newsitem.title: CHINA: China commodities brokers posted losses in '96.
newsitem.headline: China commodities brokers posted losses in '96.

text.p: China's commodities brokers posted dismal results this year with as many as 80 percent of them losing money, the Futures Herald newspaper said.

In an article contributed by the Shanghai Cereals and Oils Exchange, the newspaper also accused China's market regulators of favouring the securities markets, saying that more attention should be given to drafting commodities regulations.

Cost cutting measures and layoffs were now common among the 330 trading houses that specialised in commodities futures as well as the 2,500 firms that traded futures but also conducted other types of business, the newspaper said in an edition seen in Beijing on Saturday.
It did not give more precise figures or the extent of the losses.
The newspaper blamed the troubles on macro-economic factors such as official restrictions on trading in some contracts, an excess number of exchanges and undercapitalised brokerages.
But it said a key requirement for the future development of the market was greater attention to its legal strcuture.
"Without a doubt, government policy is giving priority to the development of the securities market," said the article.
It said attention was focused on the regulatory environment and the legal foundation for trading securities but the focus for commodities futures was merely a shakeout of the existing market.
China has slapped restrictions on numerous contracts from oil to sugar on fears that heavy speculation in futures was disrupting prices on the cash markets.
Once an acceptable legal structure was in place there could be a return to trading in some contracts that had been stopped due to excessive speculation, the article said.
